$comment: Golden fixtures for the Lunora wire value codec (shared/wire-codec.ts).
`cases[].encoded` is the canonical JSON wire form. A conforming codec MUST
satisfy `encode(decode(encoded)) == encoded`, which exercises both the decode
of tagged tokens and their re-encode.
A few shapes are legitimately NOT fixed points of that identity — a bare
`[TAG]` array is escaped on the way back out; an object field that arrives
as the `undefined` tag is dropped, matching JSON.stringify; a `bytes` tag
naming an unknown typed-array ctor decodes to raw bytes and re-encodes
without the name; and a `map` carrying a duplicate key collapses last-wins,
because the reference decodes into a real Map. Those carry `reencoded`, and
the assertion becomes `encode(decode(encoded)) == reencoded`. Without it
those shapes were untestable, so no port was held to them — four decoded
the first two differently, and all eight kept the unknown ctor name and
both duplicate entries.
`rejected[]` is the other half: wire values every port MUST refuse to decode.
It is data for the same reason the case list is — a rejection each suite
hard-codes for itself is a rejection only some suites have. The base64 entries
are what a lenient hand-rolled decoder lets through: the reference decodes via
`atob`, which fails any input whose length is 1 mod 4 once ASCII whitespace is
removed, so a truncated or padding-corrupted payload is an error rather than
valid-looking short bytes. (Whitespace INSIDE the payload is not here: `atob`
strips it, so the reference accepts it and a fixture demanding rejection would
be asserting against the reference.)
The rest of `rejected[]` is what a hand-rolled decoder waves through where
the reference throws: a map entry that is not EXACTLY a pair (reading slots
0 and 1 out of a longer one is the same invention as inventing a missing
half); a `set`/`arr` payload that is not an array (a string iterates per
CHARACTER); a typed-array payload that is not a whole number of elements
(`new Float32Array` on 3 bytes raises a RangeError); an `error` tag whose
props slot is missing or null (`Object.keys` throws on both); and a bigint
tag with a missing or non-ASCII digit string (`\d` is ASCII-only, while a
Unicode-aware digit test accepts Arabic-Indic ٣).
A tag's payload slot is TYPE-CHECKED, never coerced: a `date` epoch that is
not a number (`null` coerces to epoch 0 and a string to an Invalid Date), a
`bytes` payload that is not a string (`atob(null)` decodes the base64 of
"null" — three invented bytes), and a `url` href that is not a string (a
one-element array ToStrings into a parseable href). Each of those decoded,
and re-encoded as a plausible value, which is what makes them worse than a
throw; every port already refused them.
Language-native construction checks (e.g. bigint 7 -> the bigint tag, or an
integer past the exact-float64 range being refused) live in each SDK's own
suite, keyed by protocol/conformance-cases.json, since native values are not
uniformly JSON-representable.
